title: Mapo Tofu
subtitle: silken tofu in a spiced, numbing sauce of doubanjiang and Sichuan peppercorns
excerpt: Mapo tofu is a Sichuan classic: silken tofu simmered in a deeply savoury sauce built on doubanjiang, fermented black beans, and ground pork, finished with Sichuan peppercorns for heat and the distinctive numbing sensation. Serves 4 in 30 minutes.
sourceNotes: Mapo tofu (麻婆豆腐) originates in Chengdu, Sichuan province. It is attributed to a pockmarked woman (mápó) who ran an inn near a slaughterhouse in the Qing dynasty; the dish was recorded by Qing-era writers. Fu Pei-mei, Pei Mei's Chinese Cook Book (1969), gives a version with minced pork, doubanjiang, and Sichuan peppercorns that remains the template for modern reproductions. Fuchsia Dunlop, Land of Plenty (2001), provides a widely used English-language account of the Sichuan version.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sauce base can be made 2 days ahead without the tofu. Add fresh tofu when reheating.

glossaryTerms.definition: Fermented broad bean and chilli paste from Sichuan, the foundation of mapo tofu and many other Sichuan dishes. Pixian doubanjiang, aged in earthenware crocks, has the deepest flavour. Available in Asian supermarkets and online. Lee Kum Kee makes a widely available version; Pixian brands are superior.

The dried husks of the prickly ash tree, not a true pepper. They produce a numbing, tingling sensation on the tongue (má) alongside a floral, citrus-like aroma. Toast briefly in a dry pan and grind just before use for the strongest effect.

Whole soybeans fermented with salt until soft, pungent, and deeply savoury. Used in small amounts to add umami to stir-fries and braises. Rinse lightly before use. Available dried or in jars in Asian supermarkets.

Use the most silken tofu you can find. It will look fragile but holds together in the sauce if you slide it in gently and do not stir aggressively. A starch slurry thickens the sauce to a glossy coat that clings to each cube.

Bring a pan of lightly salted water to the boil. Slide in the tofu cubes and simmer for 2 minutes to firm them slightly. Drain carefully and set aside.

Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of vegetable oil in a wok over a high heat until smoking. Add {{pork-mince}} of pork mince and stir-fry, breaking it up, for 3 minutes until browned and crisp at the edges. Push to the side.

Add the doubanjiang and fermented black beans to the clear part of the wok. Stir-fry for 1 minute until the paste darkens and smells fragrant and slightly smoky. Add the garlic and ginger and stir-fry for another 30 seconds.

Pour in {{chicken-stock}} of stock and {{soy-sauce-light}} of soy sauce. Stir everything together. Gently slide in the tofu. Bring to a simmer and cook for 3 minutes, spooning sauce over the tofu without stirring.
Give the cornflour slurry a stir and pour about two-thirds of it into the wok, stirring gently. Wait 30 seconds and add more if the sauce is still too thin. It should coat the back of a spoon.
Remove from the heat. Drizzle over {{sesame-oil}} of sesame oil and scatter the ground Sichuan peppercorns over the top. Serve immediately over steamed rice, topped with sliced spring onions.

items.cause: Stirred too vigorously or tofu too silken
items.fix: Use a spoon to fold the sauce over the tofu rather than stirring. Blanching the tofu first helps it hold its shape.

items.cause: Doubanjiang and soy sauce vary in saltiness
items.fix: Taste before adding soy sauce. Different brands of doubanjiang have different salt levels . add soy sauce gradually.
Toast peppercorns in a dry pan just before grinding. They lose potency quickly once ground. Use freshly bought peppercorns if the dish has no sensation.

content.text: Mapo tofu is a home dish in Sichuan and across China. It is eaten on weekdays over rice. Restaurant versions often amplify the chilli and peppercorn levels; home versions are milder and can be adjusted to taste. A vegetarian version replaces the pork with finely diced mushrooms and uses vegetable stock without losing much.
